authors: Moody, J. Carroll; Fite, Gilbert C.
title: The Credit Union Movement: Origins and Development, 1850-1970
notes: Lincoln, Nebraska. ix + 369 pp. per catalogue records and the Business History Review / Journal of Economic History reviews. Checked at: https://libcat.library.tamu.edu/Record/in00000454219
about: The standard scholarly history of the credit union movement, tracing it from its European cooperative roots (Raiffeisen, Schulze-Delitzsch, Desjardins in Quebec) through the U.S. campaign led by Edward Filene and Roy Bergengren, the spread of state credit union laws, the Federal Credit Union Act of 1934 and the movement's growth up to 1970.

title: Crusade: The Fight for Economic Democracy in North America, 1921-1945
notes: New York. 379 pp. Written in collaboration with Agnes C. Gartland and James W. Brown (per catalogue record). A participant's account; treat as a primary source. Checked at: https://catalog.hathitrust.org/Record/010685908
about: A first-hand account by the managing director of the Credit Union National Extension Bureau (founded 1921 with Edward Filene's backing) and later of the Credit Union National Association, describing the campaign to pass state credit union laws, the Federal Credit Union Act and the organisation of the movement through 1945. It presents credit unions as a form of 'economic democracy' for working people.

title: Federal Credit Union Act (Act of June 26, 1934, ch. 750, Public No. 467, 73rd Congress)
notes: Senate bill S. 1639, introduced by Sen. Morris Sheppard of Texas; signed by President Franklin D. Roosevelt on June 26, 1934. Codified at 12 U.S.C. 1751 et seq. Cite as 48 Stat. 1216.
about: The statute that authorised the federal chartering of credit unions, defining them as cooperative associations organised to promote thrift among members and create a source of credit for provident or productive purposes, with membership limited to groups sharing a common bond of occupation or association, or residents of a well-defined neighbourhood, community or rural district.

title: Banking Act of 1933 (Act of June 16, 1933, ch. 89, Public Law 73-66)
notes: Commonly called the Glass-Steagall Act after Sen. Carter Glass and Rep. Henry B. Steagall. Short title confirmed at 12 U.S.C. 227; National Archives copy at docsteach.org (NAID 299834).
about: The New Deal banking statute that created federal deposit insurance (through what became the FDIC), separated commercial from investment banking, and tightened federal regulation of banks after the bank failures of 1930-1933.

title: A Monetary History of the United States, 1867-1960
notes: Published for the National Bureau of Economic Research. Chapter 7, 'The Great Contraction, 1929-33', was later issued separately. DOI is for the De Gruyter e-book edition. Checked at: https://www.degruyterbrill.com/document/doi/10.1515/9781400846856/html
about: A monetary history of the U.S. whose chapter on 'The Great Contraction' argues that the Federal Reserve failed to counter successive waves of bank failures, allowing the money stock to collapse and turning a recession into the Great Depression.

title: The Banking Panics of the Great Depression
notes: Series: Studies in Monetary and Financial History. 174 pp. Checked at: https://resolve.cambridge.org/core/books/the-banking-panics-of-the-great-depression/DDD1571DCF818DBCECB35419CD463D1E
about: A narrative reconstruction of the five U.S. banking panics of 1930-1933, examining their geographic spread by Federal Reserve district and the conduct of Federal Reserve officials. Wicker finds the panics were more regional than national in character (e.g., the 1930 panic was concentrated where the Caldwell banking group operated) and revises several standard accounts.

title: Nonmonetary Effects of the Financial Crisis in the Propagation of the Great Depression
notes: Earlier version: NBER Working Paper 1054 (1983). UNCONFIRMED: JSTOR stable URL https://www.jstor.org/stable/1808111 was cited by a secondary page but not opened.
about: Argues that the bank failures and debtor insolvencies of 1930-33 disrupted the 'credit intermediation' services banks provided, making credit costlier and scarcer, especially for households, farmers and small firms, and that this non-monetary channel deepened and prolonged the Depression beyond what the fall in the money stock alone explains.

title: A Reinterpretation of the Banking Crisis of 1930
about: Uses balance-sheet data for individual banks to argue that the 1930 failures were driven by both real and monetary factors, that many failing banks were small banks already weakened by regulation and regional (especially agricultural) distress, and that the 1930 failures did not differ in character from failures of the 1920s.

title: Categories and Causes of Bank Distress during the Great Depression, 1929-1933: The Illiquidity versus Insolvency Debate Revisited
notes: Related NBER Working Paper 12717.
about: Using Federal Reserve records of the cause of each bank suspension, finds that both illiquidity (runs and heavy withdrawals) and insolvency mattered: nearly three-quarters of banks that closed for financial reasons were insolvent, while heavy withdrawals were a primary cause of nearly half of all suspensions.

title: Monetary Intervention Mitigated Banking Panics during the Great Depression: Quasi-Experimental Evidence from a Federal Reserve District Border, 1929-1933
notes: Earlier version NBER Working Paper 12591 (2006). DOI taken from a bibliographic record, not from the publisher's page.
about: Compares Mississippi banks in the Atlanta Federal Reserve District, which lent freely to troubled banks in 1930, with those in the St. Louis District, which did not; banks on the Atlanta side survived at higher rates and lending and commerce contracted less, showing that central-bank intervention could mitigate panics.

authors: Calomiris, Charles W.; White, Eugene N.
title: The Origins of Federal Deposit Insurance
container: The Regulated Economy: A Historical Approach to Political Economy, ed. Claudia Goldin and Gary D. Libecap
notes: Book chapter (chap. 5) in an NBER conference volume; free PDF at https://www.nber.org/chapters/c6575.pdf.
about: Explains the adoption of federal deposit insurance in 1933 as the outcome of interest-group politics: small unit banks and their congressional allies, notably Rep. Henry Steagall, pushed for insurance that protected the unit-banking system, despite the poor record of earlier state deposit-insurance schemes and opposition from larger banks and the Roosevelt administration.

title: The Banking Crisis of 1933
notes: Lexington. x + 270 pp. (per Business History Review review). Based on the author's Columbia University dissertation. Checked at: https://uknowledge.uky.edu/upk_economics/3
about: The first full-length study of the 1933 banking crisis, examining how the nation reached the collapse of early 1933, the relations between Herbert Hoover and Franklin D. Roosevelt during the interregnum, the national bank holiday, and the emergency and reform legislation that followed.

title: Freedom from Fear: The American People in Depression and War, 1929-1945
notes: Oxford History of the United States series. Pulitzer Prize for History, 2000. Checked at: https://www.pulitzer.org/winners/david-m-kennedy
about: A comprehensive narrative history of the United States through the Great Depression and the Second World War, including the banking collapse, the Hoover and Roosevelt responses, and the New Deal's reforms, which Kennedy reads as aimed above all at creating economic security for ordinary Americans.

title: Financing the American Dream: A Cultural History of Consumer Credit
notes: xv + 377 pp. Checked at: https://press.princeton.edu/node/21122
about: Argues that the image of a debt-free, thrifty American past is a myth: Americans borrowed long before the 'credit revolution', but between 1890 and 1940 consumer credit was institutionalised and legitimised, with the 1920s spread of instalment credit (driven by the automobile industry) as the watershed. Calder contends that regular repayment imposed its own discipline rather than simply eroding thrift.

title: Buy Now, Pay Later: Advertising, Credit, and Consumer Durables in the 1920s
notes: Chapel Hill. viii + 424 pp. Checked at: https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/business-history-review/article/abs/buy-now-pay-later-advertising-credit-and-consumer-durables-in-the-1920s-bymartha-l-olney-chapel-hill-university-of-north-carolina-press-1991-viii-424-pp-tables-graphs-appendix-notes-bibliography-and-index-4500-isbn-0807819581/4EEA7D8FE611876FC4434FA5773215BB
about: A quantitative economic history concluding that a genuine revolution in household purchases of consumer durables occurred in the 1920s, and attributing it largely to supply-side changes: manufacturers' advertising and the spread of instalment credit through sales finance companies.

title: Debtor Nation: The History of America in Red Ink
notes: Series: Politics and Society in Twentieth-Century America. 378 pp. Checked at: https://studyofcapitalism.harvard.edu/publications/debtor-nation-history-america-red-ink
about: Traces personal debt in twentieth-century America from a marginal to a mainstream practice, arguing that rising indebtedness resulted not from cultural decline but from structural changes in American capitalism, shaped by federal policy (including New Deal housing and credit programmes), financial innovation and retail competition that made consumer lending profitable.

authors: Carruthers, Bruce G.; Guinnane, Timothy W.; Lee, Yoonseok
title: Bringing "Honest Capital" to Poor Borrowers: The Passage of the U.S. Uniform Small Loan Law, 1907-1930
notes: Winter 2012 issue.
about: Examines the spread of the Russell Sage Foundation's Uniform Small Loan Law, which licensed lenders to make small loans to wage earners at rates above usury ceilings in order to displace loan sharks; by the 1930s about two-thirds of states had adopted it. Econometric analysis shows that urbanisation, state economic characteristics and banking structure shaped adoption, while party politics mattered little.

title: Regulation of the Small Loan Business
notes: New York. Final volume of the Russell Sage Foundation Small Loan Series. A contemporary (primary) source. Checked at: https://www.russellsage.org/sites/default/files/Regulation-Small-Loan-Business.pdf
about: A contemporary study of small-loan lending to wage earners, covering the history of lending, the character of unregulated 'loan shark' lending, the development of small-loan legislation, the characteristics of borrowers, and the question of the maximum permissible rate of charge.

title: Consumer Credit and Economic Stability
notes: New York. Nugent directed the Foundation's Department of Consumer Credit Studies. A contemporary (primary) source. Checked at: https://www.russellsage.org/sites/default/files/Consumer-Credit-Economic-Stability.pdf
about: Treats consumer credit as a factor in economic fluctuations, providing year-end estimates of outstanding consumer credit by type for 1923-1937 and a history of consumer credit in the United States from before the Civil War into the twentieth century.

title: Making a New Deal: Industrial Workers in Chicago, 1919-1939
notes: Bancroft Prize, 1991. A second edition with a new preface appeared in 2014. Checked at: https://historywinterreadinglist.hsites.harvard.edu/news/making-new-deal-industrial-workers-chicago-1919-1939
about: Explains how Chicago's ethnically divided industrial workers became unionists and New Deal Democrats by the mid-1930s. When the Depression overwhelmed the ethnic institutions (benefit societies, ethnic banks, local stores) and welfare capitalism they had relied on, workers turned to the federal state and the CIO for security.

title: The Economics of the Credit Union
notes: Detroit. 182 pp. Author's full name per catalogue: John Tougas Croteau (1910-2007). UNCONFIRMED: the 'about' summary is inferred from title and catalogue subject data; no review or table of contents was consulted. Checked at: https://libcat.library.tamu.edu/Record/in00000053985
about: An economic analysis of the credit union as a financial institution, covering how credit unions gather members' savings and make small consumer loans and how they fit within the wider system of consumer finance.

title: On Doing Local History
notes: American Association for State and Local History series; first edition 1986, second 2003. Imprint given variously as Rowman & Littlefield or AltaMira. Checked at: https://www.abebooks.com/9780759123700/Doing-Local-History-Third-Edition-0759123705/plp
about: A reflective guide to the practice of local history, discussing the local historian's audience and responsibilities, the use and limits of local sources, the treatment of conflict and uncomfortable topics in a community's past, and how local history connects to broader historical questions.

authors: Kyvig, David E.; Marty, Myron A.
title: Nearby History: Exploring the Past Around You
notes: First edition 1982 (AASLH), second 2000. UNCONFIRMED: one catalogue gives the publisher of the 3rd edition as Rowman & Littlefield (AltaMira's parent). Checked at: https://news.drake.edu/?p=2657
about: A practical guide to researching the history of communities, families and institutions, covering published and unpublished documents, institutional records, oral history, artefacts, buildings and landscapes, and digital tools.

title: Archive Stories: Facts, Fictions, and the Writing of History
notes: Edited volume. Most catalogues give 2005; Duke's own page and Project MUSE give January 2006. Checked at: https://www.dukeupress.edu/archive-stories
about: Essays on how archives are created, accessed and experienced, and how those conditions shape the histories written from them; contributors examine official archives, counter-archives, oral histories and other unconventional sources, treating the archive as a historical artefact rather than a neutral repository.

title: Dust: The Archive and Cultural History
notes: Encounters series. Published in the U.S. by Rutgers University Press (2002). Manchester University Press's own page gives January 2002; the Warwick repository record gives 2001. Checked at: https://wrap.warwick.ac.uk/37701
about: A meditation on the archive and the practice of history, responding to Derrida's 'archive fever'. Steedman argues that the archive holds only fragments, the 'dust' of the past, and that history is made from what the historian does with these partial, often mundane records rather than from a complete record.

title: Silencing the Past: Power and the Production of History
notes: Boston. 191 pp. A twentieth-anniversary edition with a foreword by Hazel V. Carby was published later. Checked at: https://nationalhumanitiescenter.org/fellows-book/silencing-the-past-power-and-the-production-of-history
about: Argues that silences enter historical production at four moments: the making of sources, the making of archives, the making of narratives and the making of history in the final instance. These silences reflect unequal power. Case studies include the Haitian Revolution, the Alamo and Columbus commemorations.

title: The Voice of the Past: Oral History
notes: New York. xii + 484 pp. Oxford Oral History Series. Earlier editions by Thompson alone: 1978, 1988, 2000. Checked at: https://ioha.org/the-voice-of-the-past-oral-history-fourth-edition/
about: A classic introduction to oral history covering its development, its value for recovering the experience of ordinary people and communities, questions of memory and evidence, and the practical methods of interviewing, recording, archiving and interpretation.

title: Historians Who Love Too Much: Reflections on Microhistory and Biography
notes: June 2001 issue.
about: Distinguishes microhistory from biography. Biography values an individual life for its own uniqueness and significance, while microhistory studies a single, often obscure, life or episode as an allegory illuminating the wider culture. The essay reflects on the historian's attachment to subjects in both forms.
